query: For AlCrFeNiSi powder feedstock intended for additively manufactured miniature components, what single intervention could overcome the residual thermal stresses, degraded mechanical properties, and processing complexity associated with mainstream metallic additive-manufacturing regimes? Formulate one hypothesis that specifies the intervention and mechanism, predicts outcomes relative to components made under conventional high-thermal-load additive-manufacturing conditions, states the applicable processing window, geometry, and test conditions, identifies supporting prior evidence, and describes a falsification experiment.

generation.hypothesis: A post‐process ultrasonic peening treatment applied to laser‐additively manufactured AlCrFeNiSi components will convert tensile residual stresses into compressive stresses, thereby enhancing fatigue performance and overall mechanical integrity.
generation.material_initial_state: As-built AlCrFeNiSi miniature components produced via conventional high-thermal-load AM processes that exhibit tensile residual stresses and a heterogeneous microstructure, especially near the surfaces.
generation.intervention: Apply an automated ultrasonic peening treatment with controlled amplitude (approximately 30–50 μm) and frequency (around 20 kHz) uniformly across the entire surface of the component.
generation.conditions: Post-fabrication treatment carried out at room temperature under controlled settings to achieve uniform plastic deformation on the component surfaces to a depth of approximately 2 mm, suitable for miniature geometries.
generation.structural_mediator: The creation of a near-surface compressive stress layer combined with refined dislocation structures, enhancing fatigue resistance and mitigating crack initiation.
generation.mechanism: High-frequency mechanical peening induces localized plastic deformation that converts tensile residual stresses into compressive stresses, reducing the driving force for crack initiation and improving fatigue life.
generation.predicted_outcome: A shift in surface residual stresses from approximately +50 MPa to around –150 MPa, resulting in a significant improvement in fatigue life and a more uniform stress distribution within the treated near-surface regions.
generation.baseline: Untreated components produced under standard laser AM conditions, characterized by high tensile residual stresses and an increased risk of fatigue-induced failure due to thermal stress accumulation.
generation.boundary: This method is primarily effective for near-surface stress modification (up to about 2 mm depth), and may not fully address internal residual stresses in thicker components.
generation.uncertainty: While ultrasonic peening is well-established for other alloys like AlSi10Mg, its direct effectiveness for high-entropy alloys like AlCrFeNiSi in miniature, complex geometries requires further targeted research to confirm treatment uniformity and long-term compressive stress retention.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate identical sets of miniature components via conventional AM; subject one set to an automated ultrasonic peening treatment under the defined parameters, and leave the other set untreated. Measure surface and sub-surface residual stress profiles (using XRD and incremental hole drilling) and conduct fatigue testing under cyclic loading.
measurements: Residual stress profiles before and after peening
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If post-peening measurements do not demonstrate a transformation from tensile to compressive stresses (targeting approximately –150 MPa) along with a significant improvement in fatigue life compared to the control, then the hypothesis must be rejected.

cited_evidence.text: Ultrasonic peening treatment (UPT) has been proved to be an effective way of improving residual stresses distribution in weld structures. Thus, it shows a great potential in stress modification for metal parts fabricated by additive manufacturing technology. In this paper, an investigation into the ultrasonic treatment process of AlSi10Mg specimens fabricated by selective laser melting (SLM) process was conducted by means of experimental and numerical simulation. The specimens were prepared using a SLM machine, and UPT on their top surface was carried out. The residual stresses were measured with an X-ray stress diffraction device before and after UPT. Meanwhile, a finite element simulation method for analyzing the influence of UPT on the residual stress field of specimens was proposed and validated by experiments. Firstly, the thermal mechanical coupling numerical simulation of the SLM process of the specimen was carried out in order to obtain the residual stress distribution in the as-fabricated specimen. Then, the transient dynamic finite element simulation model of the UPT process of the specimen was established, and the UPT effect analysis was implemented. In the UPT simulatio

In this paper, the SLM building process of AlSi10Mg specimens, the UPT process of the specimen and the effect of UPT on the residual stress distribution were studied by means of experiment and FEM simulation. The UPT process can significantly modify the residual stresses distribution in the laser additively manufactured specimens, the tensile stresses (the maximum value 50 MPa) can be changed into compressive stresses (the minimum value −150 MPa) after UPT. An experimental study strategy and setup was presented first. A FEM method for simulating the UPT process of the specimens was proposed. Simufact Additive was used to simulate the SLM building process and predict the residual stress field. The specimen’s model file containing residual stress was processed using Simufact Forming, and then it was applied as the initial FEA model for UPT simulation in MSC Marc. Based on the initial prestressed specimen model, a dynamic finite element model of UPT established in MSC Marc was used to analyze the influence of UPT on residual stress. The material mechanical property data and constitutive model parameters required in the simulation analysis were obtained through a series of experiments.

papers.title: Evolution of Material Properties and Residual Stress with Increasing Number of Passes in Aluminium Structure Printed via Additive Friction Stir Deposi
papers.system: Aluminium alloys processed via additive friction stir deposition (AFSD)
papers.approach: Layer‐by‐layer solid‐state deposition using a stepped structure with varying numbers of passes to study microstructure, residual stress, and mechanical properties
papers.findings: AFSD avoids the melting-related issues of fusion processes, significantly reducing residual stresses; however, the deposition path, number of passes, and geometry induce variations in stress distribution and mechanical properties, with higher passes potentially leading to deformations and hardness gradients.
papers.mechanism: Solid‐state processing entails extreme plastic deformation and dynamic recrystallization that refines the grain structure without melting, thus minimizing thermal gradients; yet, thermal cycling across layers still generates localized stress variations.

papers.title: Residual Stress Reduction Technology in Heterogeneous Metal Additive Manufacturing.
papers.system: High-hardness metals (e.g., cold and hot work mold steels) fabricated by laser-based AM
papers.approach: Employing real-time preheating during the AM process and tuning laser power to reduce thermal deviation
papers.findings: Preheating the build environment from room temperature (25 °C) significantly decreased residual stresses (by up to 57%), and these changes improved overall microstructural uniformity in both small and large-area specimens.
papers.mechanism: By lowering thermal gradients during layer deposition, the transient thermal stresses are minimized, leading to reduced accumulation of residual stresses without the need for extensive post-processing.

papers.title: Investigation of the Microstructural Evolution and Mechanical Properties of the AlCoCrFeNi₂.₁ EHEA Fabricated by Additive Manuf
papers.system: Eutectic high-entropy alloys (EHEAs) similar in composition to high-multicomponent systems (parallels with AlCrFeNiSi)
papers.approach: Laser additive manufacturing combined with subsequent low-temperature heat treatment to relieve residual stresses and stabilize microstructure
papers.findings: Low-temperature heat treatments (≤900 °C) act as effective stress relief-annealing steps, reducing internal stresses while altering yield strength and microstructural features; finer eutectic spacing and phase stability were noted at lower heat treatment temperatures.
papers.mechanism: Thermal annealing induces controlled recrystallization and phase evolution that relieve built-in residual stresses, although excessive temperatures can promote grain coarsening and degrade strength.

papers.title: Modification of Residual Stresses in Laser Additive Manufactured AlSi10Mg Specimens Using an Ultrasonic Peening Technique.
papers.system: AlSi10Mg alloy produced via selective laser melting (SLM)
papers.approach: Application of post-process ultrasonic peening treatment (UPT) to modify the residual stress distribution in additively manufactured specimens
papers.findings: UPT transformed tensile residual stresses (up to +50 MPa) into compressive stresses (down to -150 MPa) and generated a more uniform stress profile, promising improved fatigue and crack-resistance properties.
papers.mechanism: High-frequency mechanical peening induces localized plastic deformation at the surface, converting tensile stresses to compressive stresses and effectively redistributing internal stresses.

The effectiveness of preheating versus mechanical interventions like ultrasonic peening can depend on the alloy system and processing geometry; what works best for one material or scale may not be optimal for another.

There is debate over whether a single thermal or mechanical intervention can universally address residual stresses, degraded properties, and processing complexity without compromising other aspects of component performance.

opportunities: Investigate an integrated low-temperature post-deposition heat treatment tailored for AlCrFeNiSi to relieve residual stresses while preserving microstructural integrity in miniature components.
Explore combining in situ preheating with rapid, controlled heat treatment cycles to minimize thermal gradients without inducing grain coarsening.

directions.direction: In situ integrated low‐temperature heat treatment during deposition
directions.type: Heat or thermomechanical treatment and microstructure control
directions.assessment: This approach uses an elevated substrate temperature (e.g., 650–700 °C) maintained during deposition to promote in situ stress relief and controlled dynamic recrystallization. It directly targets thermal gradients and residual stress accumulation while preserving fine microstructure. It is supported by low‐temperature annealing studies on similar high‐entropy alloys, though its precise window for AlCrFeNiSi must be validated. It respects the constraints of miniature components and shows promise to simplify post‐processing.

UPT converts surface tensile residual stresses into beneficial compressive stresses via high-frequency mechanical impact. It has demonstrated substantial reductions in tensile stresses (from ~+50 MPa to ~–150 MPa) in alloys like AlSi10Mg. While directly addressing residual stress and potentially improving fatigue performance, its depth of influence may be limited in miniature components and must be calibrated for the AlCrFeNiSi system.

By preheating the build environment (e.g., maintaining a chamber temperature around 400 °C), the thermal gradients during layer deposition are reduced. This intervention is known to lower residual stress formation in high‐hardness metals and promotes more uniform microstructure. However, implementation for miniature components (with high surface‐to‐volume ratios) may require stringent control.

directions.direction: Optimized low‐power, high‐speed laser scanning strategy
directions.assessment: Altering the laser processing parameters to reduce power while increasing scanning speed can decrease layer heat input, thereby lowering thermal gradients and residual stress buildup. This single‐step, process‐intrinsic intervention simplifies processing complexity. The mechanism is rooted in known relationships between laser energy, cooling rates, and microstructure evolution; however, the balance between energy input and part densification must be precisely modeled.
